name: Marsiglio's and Occam's theory of popular and conciliar sovereignty
plain_explanation: Marsiglio of Padua argued that ultimate legislative authority belongs to the majority of the people, who have the right to punish even princes, and that this popular sovereignty extends to the Church too: local councils (including laypeople) should elect representatives to General Councils, which alone should have power to excommunicate and to authoritatively interpret Scripture, leaving the Pope with no special powers and no secular authority. Occam did not go quite as far as Marsiglio but worked out a fully democratic method for electing the General Council.
precise_definition: The fourteenth-century political theory, developed chiefly by Marsiglio of Padua and adopted in modified form by Occam, that legislative and even ecclesiastical authority derives from the sovereignty of the people (including the laity), to be exercised through elected representative councils rather than through unilateral papal or imperial authority.
why_it_mattered: It marks a shift from the earlier, purely imperial form of opposition to the papacy toward a genuinely democratic one, which Russell says 'ultimately led to the Reformation,' and it directly informed the conciliar movement that resolved the Great Schism in the following century (covered in Chapter XV).
historical_origin: Developed by Marsiglio of Padua (1270-1342) in close collaboration with Occam during their shared exile under the protection of Emperor Louis of Bavaria in Munich, following their excommunication in 1328.
examples: Occam's reported remark to the Emperor: 'Do you defend me with the sword, and I will defend you with the pen.'
Occam's 'Eight Questions Concerning the Power of the Pope,' addressing burning practical political questions of the day
competing_positions: Dante's De Monarchia, which held Emperor and Pope both independently divinely appointed -- a position Russell calls already outdated
influence_on_later_thinkers: The conciliar movement it inspired healed the Great Schism at the Council of Constance (1414-18); Russell notes, however, that its aim (preserving Catholic unity through democratic means) differed from the later Protestant claim to private judgement, which rejected submission to any General Council; Occam was, of all the schoolmen, the one Luther preferred.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly political-theological: Occam and Marsiglio were excommunicated in 1328 for siding with Michael of Cesena in the Franciscan poverty dispute against Pope John XXII.
